articles.title: Gaza war sped up India’s shift towards Israel under Modi
articles.cleaned_content:
New Delhi, India – The United Kingdom, France, Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Norway had already banned the entry of Bezalel Smotrich, Israel’s far-right finance minister, who had advocated the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in Gaza and the annexation of the occupied West Bank.

But in September 2025, as the European Union was planning bloc-wide sanctions against him and his fellow far-right colleague Itamar Ben-Gvir that it would eventually announce late that month, Smotrich was welcomed with garlands and a multi-city trip to India. In New Delhi, he signed a trade deal; in Mumbai, he visited the stock exchange; and in Gujarat – the home state of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi – he travelled to a new investment hub.

As Israel was conducting its genocidal war on Gaza, bombing and killing dozens on the very days he was visiting India, New Delhi was ready to expand business with Israel like never before. For decades, India had been one of the world’s staunchest supporters of Palestine, and Europe one of Israel’s closest backers. India’s position has shifted firmly since 2014, when Modi and his Hindu majoritarian Bharatiya Janata Party came to power. But analysts say the optics of Smotrich’s visit underlined something even more dramatic: At a time when even Europe, traditionally seen as backing Israel, has veered away from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, the genocidal war on Gaza appears to have escalated India’s embrace of Israel.

In February this year, Modi visited Israel as Netanyahu – who faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court over war crimes carried out in Gaza – faced growing isolation in the international arena.

“You are a great friend of Israel. You are more than a friend. You are a brother,” Netanyahu told Modi when both leaders addressed the Israeli parliament in Jerusalem.

How October 7 attack changed tones

Three years of Israeli attacks have killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children. That is about one in every 30 people, or 3 percent of the pre-war population.

Historically, India has argued that diplomacy and dialogue are the way forward to resolve conflicts – whether between Russia and Ukraine, the US and Iran, or Israel and Palestine. New Delhi has maintained that war doesn’t solve anything.

But investigations by Al Jazeera and other reporting have revealed that New Delhi exported weapons to Israel during the ongoing genocidal war on Gaza. Meanwhile, under Modi, India has become Israel’s largest weapons buyer.

Just hours after the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, India’s Modi unequivocally condemned the “terrorist attack”, adding that he was “deeply shocked”. When he visited Israel in February this year, Modi referred to the Mumbai attacks in 2008, carried out by Pakistani fighters, which New Delhi has blamed on the Pakistani government. “Like you, we have a consistent and uncompromising policy of zero tolerance for terrorism with no double standards,” Modi said.

Analysts believe that the framing of Israel as a country under attack has helped Modi justify pushing India closer to it. For decades, much of the politics of Modi’s BJP “has hovered around Islamist expansionism or Islamic terrorism”, said Rasheed Kidwai, a political analyst in New Delhi.

“So it helps [in relationship with Israel],” Kidwai said, pointing to the link between Modi’s Israel policy and his domestic politics. “Take this relationship as an extension of the domestic narrative that one sees in India.”

The Indian Hindu right has long supported the ideology of Zionism, analysts note. Modi’s BJP has roots in a philosophy, Hindutva, which ultimately seeks to transform India into a Hindu nation and a natural homeland for Hindus anywhere in the world – similar to Israel’s view of itself as a Jewish homeland.

Since the October 7 attacks on Israel, Kidwai noted, “the anti-Muslim sentiments fill in that block in India.” This feeling is, of course, coupled with “pragmatism in New Delhi because Israel is a potent international player”.

Navdeep Suri, a former Indian diplomat who served as ambassador to Egypt and the United Arab Emirates, told Al Jazeera that people-to-people ties are also a central pillar of the India-Israel relationship, “particularly within a section of Indian society that has strong admiration for the muscular policy that Israel adopts”.

Time and again, there have been calls from within Indian right-wing echelons for Modi to adopt more Israel-like policies, from clampdowns in Indian-administered Kashmir to attacking neighbouring Pakistan.

Suri noted that a shift towards Israel predates the ongoing genocidal war in Gaza. “Under PM Modi, a relationship that was largely covert or under the carpet has become a much more open relationship,” the former Indian diplomat said.

“There has been a recognition in Delhi that Israel has been a very strong defence and intelligence partner,” he told Al Jazeera, referring to another pillar of the bilateral relationship. “There’s a genuine convergence when it comes to the perceptions on security.”

India ‘should take principled positions’

Even several of Israel’s closest European allies have moved from criticism of the genocidal war on Gaza and expansive illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank to concrete measures. At least 11 European countries and Canada have imposed trade measures against products from illegal Israeli settlements. Many have imposed sanctions on settlers and networks accused of conducting pogroms against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, as well as on ministers like Smotrich and Ben-Gvir.

India, for its part, has avoided anything more than homilies and mild opposition to war and West Bank attacks.

Diplomatically, New Delhi still backs a two-state solution and has called for aid access and peace in the region. Suri, the former Indian diplomat who served in the Middle East, said New Delhi “should be able to take more principled positions on these things”.

However, from his experience in office, Suri added, “there is such a close alignment at the political levels between the governments in Israel and India that there is a reluctance [in India] to criticise Israel.

“That reluctance manifests in various aspects,” Suri explained to Al Jazeera. “The refusal to criticise the settlers’ attacks; refusal to criticise the brutal use of force in Gaza; refusal to criticise the attack on Iran and point out violation of international norms.”

Unlike Western countries, India’s current leaders “lack that kind of dynamic thinking and are rather far more dogmatic”, said Kidwai, the political analyst.

India’s shift and Modi’s calculus

Netanyahu’s disruptive and fatal assault on Gaza has drawn ire from even the White House in Washington, where Israel enjoys bipartisan support. United States President Donald Trump has previously threatened to cut off support for Israel’s bombing of Lebanon – even while signing off on huge weapons sales to Israel.

However, nothing has moved Modi’s bonhomie with Israel’s Netanyahu.

In fact, Modi’s February visit on the eve of the joint US-Israel attacks on Iran appeared “as almost a personal favour to Netanyahu by boosting his image as an international statesman just as Israeli election campaigning is getting under way”, Max Rodenbeck, Israel/Palestine programme director at the Washington-based International Crisis Group, had told Al Jazeera.

Such an act would have been unthinkable from an Indian leader in previous decades.

In 1948, India opposed the creation of Israel. A relationship with Israel was once frowned upon in New Delhi – a legacy of India’s anti-colonial past – though the two had clandestine ties since at least the 1970s.

India backed the 1975 United Nations General Assembly resolution calling Zionism a form of racism, was the first non-Arab nation to recognise the Palestine Liberation Organization, and was among the first in the world to recognise Palestinian statehood. It only established diplomatic ties with Israel in 1992, and though governments since then slowly built up relations, Modi, in 2016, was the first Indian PM to visit that country.

The Congress party that’s now in opposition, but ruled India for most of its post-independence period before Modi, also viewed its support for Palestine as helpful with Muslim voters – only Indonesia and Pakistan have more Muslims than India – said Kidwai. Modi’s Hindu-first politics, by contrast, thrives on othering Indian Muslims.

“Modi’s party believes it stands to gain nothing from a pro-Palestine posture,” Kidwai told Al Jazeera. “Instead, Modi has sought to link the attack on Israel with the so-called reign of terror and Islamic extremism and make a case against Muslims – and within those realms lies the justification of everything.”

Israeli-Palestinian conflict live updates: Israel marks 3 years since Oct. 7 attack

Memorials are being held at homes, roadsides, kibbutzim and a music festival site.

Family members of victims of the Oct. 7 attack gather today at the Nova music festival site in Re'im, Israel. Erik Marmor / Getty

National memorial ceremony marks anniversary of  Oct. 7 attacks

Tens of thousands of people gathered at Yarkon Park in Tel Aviv to attend a national memorial ceremony to commemorate the anniversary of the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023.

Organized by the families of October 7 , the ceremony was held for the third year to mourn victims of the attacks.

“One thousand and ninety-six days of loss have passed,” said actress Shani Cohen, who co-hosted the ceremony alongside Eli Sharabi, a former hostage who lost his wife and two daughters in the attacks. “Remembering those who begged for help from within safe rooms engulfed in flames; those who hid in dumpsters, in bullet-riddled restroom stalls, and in shelters packed with people.”

Three years ago, militants led by Hamas killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. Israel’s yearslong military offensive in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 people.

Hundreds of bereaved families, hostages and survivors of the attacks participated in the ceremony, sharing their stories of grief, alongside emotional musical performances from well-known Israeli artists.

Herzog says communities hit by Oct. 7 are now rebuilding: 'We shall continue'

Israeli President Isaac Herzog spoke at the memorial ceremony held at the site of the Nova Festival near Re’im in southern Israel, where hundreds of festivalgoers were murdered and abducted during the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks three years ago.

"We are here to tell their story and to remember and reflect and reminisce in this solemn day and say to the world, we shall dance again, we shall live again," he said. "This whole region, which was attacked barbarically on October 7, is now rebuilding, and it will double its population in the next few years, and people have chosen to come here and to live here and to say yes, we shall continue."

Herzog called on the international community to support efforts to disarm Hamas and combat Iran.

“We are a nation like all nations. We have the inherent right to defend ourselves and fight terror. But we yearn for peace, and we want our neighbors to live in peace as well,” Herzog said.

Trump's Board of Peace vows no October 7 will happen again

President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace paid tribute to Israelis and Palestinians in a statement today that said it was “striving to create the conditions for a lasting peace through the demilitarization and deradicalization of Gaza.”

The body, which Trump has billed as part of the solution to a series of global conflicts, said in a statement that its effort was “defined by pragmatic solutions, not statements or slogans.”

“Genuine and durable security for Israel is the foundation on which an peace must be built, and it is the surest guarantee that no October 7 will ever happen again,” it added.

Palestinian killed in the occupied West Bank, official news agency reports

At least one Palestinian was killed and 14 injured when Jewish settlers attacked olive farmers near the town of Nablus in the occupied West Bank, the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported today.

The Palestinian Red Crescent Society said that its teams treated two people for gunshot wounds and three who had been beaten, the news agency reported.

According to the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), some 6,500 Palestinians have been displaced due to settler attacks in the West Bank since 2023.

Between Jan. 1 and July 24, Israeli forces or settlers killed 76 Palestinians, according to the latest data available from OCHA. Three Israelis were killed over the same period, the data shows.

Israeli documentary ‘NAZA’ charting Gaza killings opens in U.S.

Without a traditional distributor, a documentary that charts the Israeli military’s systematic killing of civilians, arrives in a limited number of U.S. theaters this month after sparking an intense backlash in Israel.

Israelis Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, both Academy Award-winning filmmakers, faced intense backlash at home following the documentary's premiere last month at the Venice Film Festival — where it earned an unprecedented 25-minute standing ovation.

Szor and Abraham pose with the Special Jury Prize Award at the Venice Film Festival. Rocco Spaziani / Mondadori Portfolio via Getty

The documentary, based on insider accounts from Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers, sparked outrage among Israeli officials , even spurring calls to consider criminal charges against the documentarians and strip them of their citizenship.

After showings at New York’s IFC Center, the documentary will open Oct. 9 in cities including Austin, Chicago, Los Angeles and Seattle. It will also be available to stream for free on The Guardian’s website in late November.

“I felt that we have a responsibility, from our position, to also talk to the people who did it themselves and to bring this insider testimony, hoping that this will make the denial of what is happening harder,” Abraham told NBC News last month.

The Israel Defense Forces published a 10-page rebuttal last week, claiming the documentary is “based on substantial factual errors stemming from a misrepresented and manipulative depiction of reality.”

Meanwhile, in an unusual step, Israel's Embassy in the U.S. was promoting a similarly titled documentary, "NAZA: The Real Story," which features senior IDF officials defending their conduct in Gaza.

Who has accused Israel of genocide in Gaza?

The term genocide has increasingly been used by human rights bodies and independent experts to refer to Israel's actions in Gaza following the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas, despite emphatic Israeli and American denials.

Israel has said it abides by international law and the accusation distorts the legal definition of genocide. It also contends that the war in Gaza is an existential conflict with a foe that regularly uses civilians as human shields.

More than 74,000 people have been killed across the Gaza Strip since the war began, according to figures from the Palestinian Health Ministry.

In September 2025, an independent commission established by the U.N. Human Rights Council published a report concluding that Israel had committed genocide, citing widely accepted definitions under long-standing international conventions.

“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the Genocide Convention,” said Navi Pillay, chair of the commission.

"Explicit statements by Israeli civilian and military authorities and the pattern of conduct of the Israeli security forces indicate that the genocidal acts were committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, Palestinians in the Gaza Strip as a group," the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights said in a statement at the time.

In October 2025, the U.N.'s Special Rapporteur for human rights in the Palestinian territories, Francesca Albanese, alleged that the "ongoing genocide in Gaza is a collective crime, sustained by the complicity of influential third states that have enabled longstanding systemic violations of international law by Israel."

Leading Israeli human rights organization B’Tselem also published a report in July 2025 concluding that Israel was committing genocide.

"Statements by senior Israeli officials and actions on the ground prove beyond any doubt that, in Israel’s eyes, the entire population of the Gaza Strip is the target," it said, adding to similar findings from groups including Amnesty International and Physicians for Human Rights Israel.

In November 2024, the International Criminal Court, which can try individuals for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity, issued an arrest warrant for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Yoav Gallant, alongside a warrant for deceased Hamas military commander Mohammed Deif.

The warrants did not indicate specific genocide charges, with the charges listed against Netanyahu instead including "crimes of starvation as a method of warfare and of intentionally directing an attack against the civilian population; and the crimes against humanity of murder, persecution, and other inhumane acts."

The United States and Israel do not accept the ICC's jurisdiction.

Somber crowds gather at music festival massacre site

A hush fills the place that three years ago was bursting with music and dancing.

Today, thousands of people are at the site paying their respects to those killed at the Nova music festival near Re’im in southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.

Young and old alike stood solemnly, some alone, some in small groups next to the memorials for their loved ones, which feature a picture and text describing who they were.

People light memorial candles inside a protective glass display box at the Nova music festival site today. Erik Marmor / Getty Images

Some shed tears, others seemed lost in thought as they reflected on the 364, mostly young people who were killed three years ago at the site, which sits close to the border with Gaza. Flags stood at half staff.

One man, who did not wish to be named because he is currently a soldier in the Israeli military, said he was there on the day of the attack, but he managed to get out because his father called him shortly after the attacks began and told him to get out. Seven of his friends died, he said.

Others are keen to talk about their loved ones as they feel the world has not heard enough about the suffering that was inflicted on them that day.

Hamas vows to continue fight against Israel

Hamas today vowed to continue to try and unify Palestinian factions three years after the attacks of Oct. 7, 2023.

In a lengthy statement, the militant group said the attacks it led were a response to decades of aggression by Israel and had shattered illusions about the might of the country’s military.

It vowed to continue trying to unify different Palestinians factions, or political groups.

It also called on the International Criminal Court, which issued an arrest warrant for Benjamin Netanyahu in November 2024, to prosecute the Israeli prime minister, working along with the International Court of Justice.

The statement also said that Hamas was still committed to the ceasefire deal brokered by President Donald Trump last October, while accusing Israel of not honoring the deal.

A total of 1,467 people have since been killed in Gaza despite the ceasefire came into effect, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry, which operates in the part of Gaza still run by Hamas. ‌Israel says four soldiers have ​been killed in that time.

Analysis: Flydubai hijacking attempt brings up similar questions to those asked after Oct. 7

Last week’s attempted hijacking of a Flydubai flight to Tel Aviv has Israelis asking what went wrong with their country’s security policies — the same painful question asked so many times after the Oct. 7 attacks.

The initial Israeli reaction to the incident — in which an Omani pilot allegedly attacked the flight’s captain with an axe and tried to seize control of the plane before being overpowered by passengers — was relief. A disaster had been narrowly averted and the passengers who stormed the cockpit were celebrated as heroes.

But in the days since, the public focus has shifted to what appears to be a series of security failures. Under Israeli law, foreign airlines must declare the names of their crewmembers to Israel’s Transport Ministry before they land in Tel Aviv. The Transport Ministry has now acknowledged that while it collects the names of crewmembers, it does not conduct background checks on them.

Such a background check might have detected that the co-pilot had been previously banned from flying in Oman because of his radical views, according to multiple U.S. officials, an Israeli official and a Middle Eastern diplomat.

Israel supporters confront pro-Palestinian marchers in London

A student march in support of Palestinians today in London was met by counterprotesters supporting Israel. Officials had urged students to reconsider holding the march on the third anniversary of the attacks but allowed it to go ahead with restrictions, including a ban on face coverings.

A counterprotester shouts at the marchers. Leon Neal / Getty

Police remove a student demonstrator. Ben Whitley / PA via Getty

Beach art installation 'chilling and beautiful,' Canadian couple says

Standing next to an art installation depicting the bodies of Israelis killed in the October 7 attacks, Tamara Amar called it “chilling and beautiful.”

“There’s just something so beautiful about this,” the 56-year market researcher told NBC News on Tel Aviv’s Trumpeldore Beach, where rows of human figures had been painted in black and yellow.

An installation on the beach in Tel Aviv marks the third anniversary of the Hamas attacks. Oded Balilty / AP

In some ways “what happened on October 7 is kind of our modern day holocaust,” Patrick said. “To experience it three years later, as if it just happened, it’s bone chilling.”

On the day of the attacks he said he picked up his phone and turned to Tamara and said: “Israel’s been attacked. We are at war.” He added that he “knew this was different.”

Tamara said it was the first time they had visited Israel since the massacre three years ago.

“We wanted to come so many times,” she said. adding that she “felt my soul crushed” by the events. "We're no better off than we were three years ago, and that's the part that I find you know most upsetting,” she added,

But asked about the future Patrick said: “You have to be hopeful, otherwise you’ll sink,” adding that he thought “the future was positive.”

Hard to reflect while 'political catastrophe' continues

The loved ones of many former Hamas hostages “can’t really forgive” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for his actions surrounding the Oct. 7, 2023, attack, a vocal figurehead for the families has told NBC News’ “Here’s the Scoop” podcast.

There were "so many chances to stop the war and make a deal to get hostages back and save their lives, and they were missed, and that's what's so hurtful to us," said Gil Dickmann, whose cousin Carmel Gat was killed after 328 days as a captive in Gaza.

Dickmann frequently pressed for a swift deal to secure the hostages’ release.

Netanyahu met with hostage families numerous times throughout the war, and repeatedly vowed that their return was his top priority. But Dickmann said the leader “doesn’t take any responsibility.”

Dickmann also alleges that Netanyahu "didn't want to hear any warnings about what was going on in Gaza" prior to October 7, with his focus instead on the West Bank. Hamas rule in Gaza was seen as preferable to an expanded Palestinian Authority "that may lead to a Palestinian state," he said.

Dickmann said he would mark Oct. 7 by visiting the graves of his murdered relatives, but added that it was hard to focus on memories of them "when we still have this political catastrophe still going on," referring to Netanyahu's government.

He expressed hopes that the Israeli election later this month would bring a new government that could commission an independent inquiry into Oct. 7, the events leading up to it and the war in Gaza.

Listen to the full podcast here.

Satellite imagery highlights devastation in Gaza

Recent satellite images have captured the devastation across the Gaza Strip after Israel’s yearslong military offensive.

Tal al-Sultan, near Gaza's southern city of Rafah, in 2022, 2024 and 2026. Google Earth; Google Maps

The Google satellite imagery spread on social media this month. A spokesperson for Google told NBC News it was last updated in June.

Israel has heavily restricted access to the Palestinian enclave since launching its offensive after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, with international journalists blocked from entering aside from brief and strictly controlled media tours facilitated by the Israeli military.

Flydubai case raises similar security questions to those about Oct. 7

Last week’s attempted hijacking of a Flydubai flight to Tel Aviv has Israelis asking what went wrong with their country’s security policies — the same painful question asked so many times after Oct. 7, 2023.

Passengers and crew were hailed as heroes after they managed to subdue the alleged attacker, identified by NBC News as Omani national Hamman al-Hamammi.

The co-pilot had allegedly attacked Capt. Smit Machchhar with a cabin axe before trying to take control of the aircraft’s flight controls, sending the plane plummeting.

The jet, which was carrying 174 passengers, most of them Israeli, was stabilized and landed safely in what some of those onboard have described as a "miracle."

But in the days since, the public focus has shifted to what appears to be a series of security failures.

Under Israeli law, foreign airlines must declare the names of their crew members to the Israeli Transport Ministry before they land in Tel Aviv.

The ministry has now acknowledged that while it collects the names of crewmembers, it does not conduct background checks on them.

The co-pilot accused in the attack had been previously banned from flying in Oman because of his radical views and had posted on social media about killing Jews, according to multiple U.S. officials, an Israeli official and a Middle Eastern diplomat.

Beach art installation brings back vivid memories for American woman

Trumpeldor beach in central Tel Aviv, packed and lively just yesterday, is today almost empty.

The white sand has been covered with an enormous installation commemorating the Oct. 7 attacks and designed to be visible to passengers on planes overhead as they make their final descent towards Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion airport.

It is made up of row after row of black cloth onto which life-sized figures have been painted. Yellow figures represent the hostages and white figures represent those killed.

A memorial on Trumpeldor beach in Tel Aviv today. Shira Pinson / NBC News

There are also three orange figures in memory of Shiri Bibas, 32, and her two children, Ariel, 4, and 9-month-old Kfir, who were killed in captivity in Gaza.

The scene is somber and still. Visitors and passersby slow down, take pictures, talk in low voices. The emotions are evident.

“Today it's so quiet, and it's so somber, and it's so…. You feel the sadness in the air,” Nava, a 69-year-old visiting Israel, told NBC News, her voice trembling.

“I didn't think I'd get so emotional because it's been time,” she said, adding that “to see so many bodies” laid out on the beach had an impact.

“For that many people to have been killed in one day, and so brutally,” she said. “It brings it all back how unfair and awful it is because all we want is peace.”

Fighting back the tears, she said the memory of that day three years ago was still very vivid. “We woke up in the morning, and we heard the news, and it was torture. It was absolute torture.”

Photos: Funeral for slain teen in Gaza

Mourners today gathered for Nimr Berbah’s funeral in Khan Younis, southern Gaza.  The 16-year-old was shot in the head and killed when the Israeli army opened fire near the Abu Hamid Junction, east of Khan Younis.

Mourners carry Nimr's body during his funeral in Khan Younis today. Abed Rahim Khatib / Anadolu via Getty

Relatives gather around the teen's body at Nasser Hospital. Abed Rahim Khatib / Anadolu via Getty

Funeral prayers for Nemr outside Nasser Hospital. Abed Rahim Khatib / Anadolu via Getty

There doesn't have to be a competition over suffering, grieving mother says

There “doesn’t have to be a competition of tears” between Israelis and Palestinians over who has suffered the most since the Hamas-led attacks Oct. 7, 2023, the mother of a slain hostage says.

“No one’s analyzing whose tears are the saltiest,” Rachel Goldberg-Polin told NBC News yesterday, a day before the third anniversary of the abduction of her son, Hersh Goldberg-Polin, from the Nova music festival in southern Israel.

Rachel Goldberg-Polin and her husband, Jon Polin. Greg Kahn for NBC News

“This is the way it always goes and it’s with conflict in world history and currently in this neck of the woods,” she added.

Hersh was among six hostages held by Hamas whose bodies were recovered in a tunnel under Gaza’s southern city of Rafah in September 2024. Born in the U.S., he had moved to Israel with his family when he was 7.

“As humans, we want to cheer for one team, red or blue. Pick your side,” the grieving mother said. “There are people suffering on all sides.”

“And until we make a very elevated, concerted decision that we’re not going to play into those tropes, we will continue doing this,” she added.

Solemn memorials play out as Israeli election looms

Today’s solemn memorials are playing out against the backdrop of a heated Israeli election in which the Oct. 7 attack and its aftermath is one of the main themes.

In just 20 days, Israelis will head to the polls to decide whether to return to power Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the man who led Israel on the day of the Hamas-led attacks and in the tumultuous years since.

Netanyahu’s opponents accuse him of a litany of failures before and after that fateful day. They say he unwisely allowed Qatari money to flow into Gaza in a bid to keep Hamas quiet. They accuse him of ignoring warnings from the United Arab Emirates that Hamas was planning a major attack. And they say he has rejected calls for a 9/11 Commission-style public inquiry because the findings of such an investigation would damage him politically.

An election banner reads "Netanyahu fights for everyone" near Ramallah, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank yesterday. Zain Jaafar / AFP via Getty

Netanyahu has blamed military and security chiefs for the failure to prevent the attacks and denies he received any concrete warnings from the UAE about Hamas’ plans.

His election message is that Israel has bounced back and taken the fight to Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebano, and its longtime opponent Iran.

“The state of Israel is the strongest country in the Middle East, and our enemies are weaker than ever,” he said at a Cabinet meeting yesterday.

A poll published this week by the Israeli Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem-based think tank, found 62% of Israelis say that the attacks will be a key factor in their decision on who to vote for.

But polls show neither the pro-Netanyahu nor the anti-Netanyahu bloc on a clear path to a majority in the Knesset, Israel's parliament.

In the three years since kibbutz Nir Oz was stormed by Hamas-led militants, Lucas Cunio told NBC News, he has coped but “you can never heal the trauma.”

“Sometimes I close my eyes and I see the road in the kibbutz and everything is burning and not easy,” he said, “When I go to sleep, sometimes I can see it. It’s really hard.”

Tributes outside a destroyed home in kibbutz Nir Oz last year. Ohad Zwigenberg / AP

Less than 2 miles from the fenced-off border with Gaza, Nir Oz  was one of the areas hit hardest when Hamas militants stormed through southern Israel. About a quarter of the 400 residents who lived here were killed or kidnapped, including two of Cunio's brothers, Ariel and David Cunio.

Both were freed after more than two years in captivity Oct. 13, 2025.

Cunio said he had joined a surfing club to help with his mental health.

"You really feel yourself again," he said. "You don’t think you don’t feel your just you your board and the water."

Hamas military wing praises attacks

A spokesperson for Hamas' military wing, the Qassam Brigades, offered a salute “steeped in glory and pride” to the fighters who took part in the Oct. 7 attacks.

Briefly acknowledging the “steep” price on the people of Gaza, Abu Obaida said they would be remembered for altering the face of history and the global balance of power.  Since the attack and the ensuing war in Gaza, around 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and the majority of its population driven from their homes.

Abu Obaida also praised Iran for its support, as well as militant groups such as Hezbollah in Lebanon and Yemen’s Houthi rebels.

Drones, he added, had “shattered the enemy’s peace of mind.”

Four people killed in Gaza over the past 24 hours

Four people have been killed in Gaza over the past 24 hours, according to the latest figures from the Palestinian Health Ministry in the enclave. A fifth succumbed to previous injuries, the ministry said.

A total of 1,467 people have been killed despite a ceasefire came into effect last October, according to the ministry which operates in the part of Gaza still run by Hamas. ‌Israel says four soldiers have ​been killed in that time.

A funeral ceremony last week for Palestinians recovered from the rubble of buildings in the Al-Tajj district of Gaza City. Ahmad Salem / Bloomberg via Getty

Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been ‌killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led ​fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in October 2023.

Photos: Commemorations in Tel Aviv

Israelis came together across several Tel Aviv locations this morning to pay their respects to the victims of the Oct. 7 attacks. Pictures show commuters conducting a moment of silence on the highway, the Dizengoff Fountain filled with red dye and a memorial beach installation honoring lives lost in the 2023 attacks.

2025 was the deadliest year for antisemitic attacks in three decades, ADL report shows

Last year was the deadliest year for antisemitic attacks in more than 30 years in the seven countries with the largest Jewish populations outside of Israel, according to a July report from the Anti-Defamation League.

Violent incidents in the U.S., U.K., Argentina, Australia, Canada, France and Germany were up 97% in 2025, compared to 2022, the year before the Hamas-led attack on Israel, the report found. Total antisemitic incidents were up by 136%, the report showed.

A total of 20 people were killed in antisemitic attacks last year including the 15 who were murdered in a mass shooting on Bondi Beach in the Australian city of Sydney.

Sarah Milgrim and Yaron Lischinsky. @IsraelinUSA / X

In the U.S., two Israeli Embassy staffers ​Yaron Lischinsky and Sarah Milgrim, were killed at the Capital Jewish Museum in Washington and 82-year-old Karen Diamond, who died from injuries sustained in a firebomb attack on a group of demonstrators advocating for the release of Israeli hostages.

Two men, Adrian Daulby and Melvin Cravitz, were also killed in the U.K. when a synagogue in Manchester was attacked on Yom Kippur.

Germany was found to have “the highest rate of antisemitic incidents per Jewish capita: nearly 70 per 1,000 Jewish residents in 2025,” the report said, adding that was “nearly five times Australia’s rate, six times the U.K.’s rate, and nearly 70 times the U.S. rate.”

Israeli kibbutz where 80 were killed marks the anniversary

Residents of kibbutz Kfar Aza held a memorial at 6:29 a.m. to mark the exact time Hamas militants attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.

Hamas killed 80 people and kidnapped another 19 that day from the sleepy, sun-drenched hamlet in southern Israel.

Hamas assault is 'central' issue in Israel's upcoming election, poll finds

A majority of Israelis say the 2023 Hamas assault will be a central issue for them in the country’s Oct. 27 election, according to a poll by the Israel Democracy Institute.

The poll found that the events of Oct. 7, 2023, were a “very central” or “fairly central” issue for 62% of those surveyed, including 68% of Jewish Israelis and 32% of Arab Israelis. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is seeking to stay in power, has been criticized over the lack of an official inquiry into the attacks, as well as reports that he was warned about them in advance.

“October 7 is casting a long shadow over Israel’s upcoming elections,” said Yohanan Plesner, the institute’s president. “Questions of security, accountability and whether the lessons of the attack have truly been learned will weigh heavily on many voters as they make their choice.”

The survey was conducted from Aug. 31 to Sept. 3, with 605 people interviewed in Hebrew and 150 in Arabic, the institute said.

The first anniversary without any Israeli hostages in Gaza

This is the first anniversary of the Oct. 7 attacks that there are no Israeli hostages — living or dead — still inside Gaza.

The last living hostages were returned to Israel on Oct. 13 last year, and the body of the final captive, 24-year-old police officer Ran Gvili, was recovered in January this year, bringing a formal end to Israel’s 843-day hostage crisis. As a result, this is also the first anniversary where the country is not plastered with hostage posters.

Mourners at the Nova festival site today. Erik Marmor / Getty

The posters seemed to cover nearly every free inch of wall or lamppost across Israel in the weeks after the 2023 Hamas assault, and they stayed up for years afterward. The images formed a grim honor guard in the main hallway at Ben Gurion Airport, and were the last thing a foreign visitor would see before boarding a flight home.

Now, the hostage posters are finally down. But stickers remembering some of the 1,200 people killed are still common.

Vigils are held across Australia as anniversary of Bondi Beach attack looms

Hundreds of people attended a vigil at Sydney’s Bondi Beach, where 15 people were killed in December in a shooting attack at a Hanukkah event, observing a moment of silence at 6:29 a.m. local time to mark the start of the 2023 Hamas assault on Israel.

Other commemorations are being held across the country, including pro-Palestinian vigils that have been criticized by politicians and Jewish groups. Israel’s war in Gaza has been deeply divisive in Australia, which has experienced a surge in both antisemitism and Islamophobia since the conflict began.

In a statement, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Australia “stands with the Jewish community here and across the world.”

“We stand against antisemitism and racism in all its forms because it goes against who we are,” he said, calling for the disarmament of Hamas and progress toward a two-state solution.

Albanese said the approaching first anniversary of the Bondi Beach attack “compounds the pain” of those commemorating the Hamas assault.

“For so many, no day since has been easy, but anniversaries fall with their own terrible weight,” he said.

Mourners gather at Nova music festival on third anniversary of Oct. 7 attack

Mourners remembered their lost loved ones at the Nova music festival site near kibbutz Reim, southern Israel, this morning to commemorate the third anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, terror attacks.

Raz Zarfati, sister of Ron Zarfati, who was killed at the Nova music festival. Ohad Zwigenberg / AP

The mother of Israeli American Hersh Goldberg-Polin who was found dead in Gaza almost 11 months after he was taken from the Nova music festival on Oct. 7, 2023, told NBC News the grief “doesn’t get better.”

“It might get different,” said Rachel Goldberg-Polin. “I’m hopeful that it will get different.”

But the “reality of what happens is that time makes you more hungry or more thirsty for your person,” she said.

Hersh Goldberg-Polin with his parents, Rachel and Jonathan. Courtesy Goldberg-Polin family

Hersh was among six hostages held by Hamas whose bodies were recovered in a tunnel under Gaza's southern city of Rafah in September 2024. Born in the U.S. he moved to Israel with his family when he was seven.

Goldberg-Polin feared the grief was “going to get worse” because “that yearning, that longing, that craving is forever,” she said.

“A couple of weeks ago, I was just crumpled on the floor and I was crying, and my daughter said to me that she came across me and she said, ‘What happened?’”

“I just looked up and I said, ‘I haven’t seen my son in three years.’”

Israelis abroad told to exercise 'heightened vigilance'

Israel's National Security Council has warned Israelis living abroad to exercise "heightened vigilance" amid an "increased risk of attempted attacks against Israelis and Jews abroad," on the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 attacks.

In a statement issued by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office, the public was urged to "refrain from posting details about travel plans abroad on social media in advance," as well as "posting content on social media that indicates service in the security forces."

Travelers were also urged to avoid traveling to Jordan, Qatar, Somaliland and Egypt and "minimize speaking Hebrew in crowded areas."

Extraordinary thing about my son was he was 'totally ordinary,' grieving mom says

The extraordinary thing about her son was that he was “totally ordinary,” the mother of Israeli American hostage Hersh Goldberg-Polin told NBC News.

Three years after he was taken from the Nova music festival in southern Israel, Rachel Goldberg-Polin said there was “always a temptation, especially when young people are killed in tragic ways, to mythologize them or lionize them.”

But for her, Hersh “was the perfect match,” she said.

Hersh was among six hostages held by Hamas whose bodies were recovered in a tunnel under Gaza’s southern city of Rafah in September 2024. Born in the U.S., he moved to Israel with his family when he was seven.

“I think what’s extraordinary about Hersh is that he is totally ordinary,” Goldberg-Polin said, adding that he was “filled with beauty and filled with flaws.”

Rachel Goldberg in 2024. Vanessa Leroy / NBC News

Israel begins commemorations with a nationwide moment of silence

Israel marked the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 attacks with a nationwide moment of silence at 6:29 a.m. local time (11:29 p.m. Tuesday ET), the exact time the Hamas assault began in 2023.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog and first lady Michal Herzog lighting a memorial candle at the president’s residence in Jerusalem this morning. Office of President Herzog

At the president’s residence in Jerusalem, President Isaac Herzog and first lady Michal Herzog lit a memorial candle to open the day’s commemorative events.

# Three Years after 7 October: What Prospects for Israel and Palestine?

*   [MED](https://www.ispionline.it/en/category/med)[Med this Week](https://www.ispionline.it/en/category/med-this-week-en)[Middle East and North Africa](https://www.ispionline.it/en/research/middle-east-and-north-africa) by [Antonia Ricciardiello](https://www.ispionline.it/en/bio/antonia-ricciardiello)

*   [](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.ispionline.it/en/publication/three-years-after-7-october-what-prospects-for-israel-and-palestine-247720 "Condividi su Facebook")[](https://twitter.com/share?url=https://www.ispionline.it/en/publication/three-years-after-7-october-what-prospects-for-israel-and-palestine-247720 "Condividi su Twitter")[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https://www.ispionline.it/en/publication/three-years-after-7-october-what-prospects-for-israel-and-palestine-247720 "Condividi su LinkedIn")[](https://telegram.me/share/url?url=https://www.ispionline.it/en/publication/three-years-after-7-october-what-prospects-for-israel-and-palestine-247720&text=Guarda%20questo%20articolo%20dalla%20pagina%20web%20di%20ISPI "Condividi su Telegram")[](https://api.whatsapp.com/send?text=Three+Years+after+7+October%3A+What+Prospects+for+Israel+and+Palestine%3F+https%3A%2F%2Fwww.ispionline.it%2Fen%2Fpublication%2Fthree-years-after-7-october-what-prospects-for-israel-and-palestine-247720 "Condividi su WhatsApp")[](mailto:?subject=Guarda%20questo%20articolo%20dalla%20pagina%20web%20di%20ISPI&body=Three%20Years%20after%207%20October:%20What%20Prospects%20for%20Israel%20and%20Palestine?%20%20https://www.ispionline.it/en/publication/three-years-after-7-october-what-prospects-for-israel-and-palestine-247720 "Condividi per Email")

The MED This Week newsletter provides informed insights on the most significant developments in the MENA region, bringing together unique opinions and reliable foresight into future scenarios. Today we take stock of the key developments in Israel and Palestine since 7 October 2023 and assess the prospects for what lies ahead.

Three years have passed since 7 October 2023: the deadliest day in Israel’s history, the beginning of the war on Gaza and the spark that set the whole Middle East on a path of violence from which it has yet to emerge. This third anniversary comes **less than three weeks ahead of the elections for the Knesset on 27 October**, the first time Israel goes to the polls since the attack, and amid growing calls for accountability for the security failures surrounding the events of 7 October. Indeed, [recent reports](https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/israel-security/2026-10-07/ty-article-magazine/.premium/all-the-warnings-netanyahu-got-before-october-7-that-we-know-of/000001a1-1604-dba5-a5bf-df44dbe70000) alleging that the UAE and Egypt provided early warnings of an impending assault to Benjamin Netanyahu have put further pressure on the prime minister as he already faces accusations from opposition figures and broad segments of the public over his responsibility for what happened on that day. Whether this will have any bearing on the closely contested race for the premiership remains to be seen. What is clear, however, is that **discussions over the responsibility for Israel’s conduct in Gaza – and in the West Bank – have been largely absent** from the electoral debate. Throughout these three years, indeed, the humanitarian devastation has been unprecedented: more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed as a result of the Israeli offensive in Gaza, including at least 21,000 children, according to the [Palestinian Ministry of Health,](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/7/three-years-of-israels-genocide-in-gaza-in-numbers) while [82% of the buildings in the Strip](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/08/1168138) have been damaged or destroyed. These developments have significantly heightened international concern, prompting a [UN Commission of Inquiry](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c0jy96w6pw2o) to conclude that Israel has committed genocide against the Palestinian population in Gaza. Nonetheless, **little has changed on the ground**. The October 2025 ceasefire has failed to bring an end to the violence, with at least [1,460 people reportedly killed](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/7/three-years-of-israels-genocide-in-gaza-in-numbers) since it took effect, while Israel continues to control more than [60% of the Strip](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/5/28/israels-netanyahu-directs-army-to-seize-70-percent-of-gaza-strip). United States President Donald Trump’s proposed roadmap to peace has largely stalled, with the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) still unable to enter the enclave. This is compounded by seemingly unchecked settler violence in the West Bank, which has increased sharply since 7 October 2023, with [2026 already the deadliest year on record](https://acleddata.com/expert-comment/settler-violence-getting-worse-west-bank) for Palestinians. In this context, in which **Palestinian agency remains structurally constrained** and deep divisions persist among political factions, it is unlikely that the elections announced for 28 November in Palestinian Territories will prove decisive in producing a united and legitimate leadership. Perhaps most significant, however, is the broader political climate in which these developments are unfolding. Recent polling shows **growing pessimism among both Israelis and Palestinians about the prospects of a two-state solution**. If coexistence already seemed like a distant possibility before 7 October, after three years of conflict it appears further out of reach than ever before.[](https://www.ispionline.it/en/publication/three-years-after-7-october-what-prospects-for-israel-and-palestine-247720)

_Experts from the ISPI network discuss the situation on the ground three years after 7 October and assess future prospects for Israel and Palestine._

## A region still in crisis

“7 October 2023 marked a decisive rupture. In Israel, it shattered the country’s sense of security and its image of invulnerability. In Gaza, it unleashed a humanitarian catastrophe and destruction on an immense scale, the consequences of which will impact generations of Palestinians to come. Across the Middle East, it upended long-standing regional balances, ushering in a period of prolonged instability and uncertainty that is affecting the entire region, from the Levant to the Gulf. Three years on, the outlook remains bleak. As Israel prepares for elections whose outcome is still uncertain, amid protests by those demanding clarity and accountability over the events of 7 October, Gaza’s population continues to endure severe deprivation and dire sanitary conditions, with reconstruction remaining nothing more than a distant dream.”

[_Valeria Talbot_](https://www.ispionline.it/it/bio/valeria-talbot)_, ISPI MENA Centre_

## Meaningful reconstruction in Gaza requires Palestinian ownership

“Very limited progress has been made towards the reconstruction of Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire. While the NCAG presented a six-month recovery program at the UN General Assembly meetings in September, it remains unclear how its projects will be financed or implemented, as NCAG members are prevented by Israel from entering Gaza. More importantly, a key challenge ahead is to ensure that Palestinians have control over the governing and financing of reconstruction. US-backed ‘day after’ plans have largely envisioned a reconstruction process that is neither driven by the people of Gaza nor accountable to them: governance is externally imposed through the Board of Peace; Palestinian political agency is undermined; and Gaza is seen as an investment opportunity for the benefit of private capital. Meaningful reconstruction will require Palestinian ownership of the process, with Palestinians exercising political agency over its priorities, governance and financing.”

[_Nur Arafeh_](https://arabcenterdc.org/team/nur-arafeh/)_, Head of the Political Economy Program and Senior Fellow, Arab Center Washington DC_

## Accountability for 7 October: what is at stake in the election?

“Netanyahu avoids taking responsibility for 7 October. He prevents a State Commission of Inquiry from being established. And he puts the blame for that horrible day’s failures on the security establishment. But reality turns out to be strikingly different from how Netanyahu portrays it. Israeli security chiefs repeatedly warned him of possible mass escalation. This has already been revealed. Now, Israelis know that warnings were also conveyed by high-level Palestinian, Egyptian and Emirati figures. Yet Netanyahu failed to act and protect Israel and its citizens. Most Israelis yearn for new leadership following the upcoming election. Alas, ideological divisions within the opposition and wrongful objection by some parties to form a coalition supported by Arab parties make this goal more difficult to attain. Recent reports about the advance warnings should remind Israelis what is at stake, mobilise opposition supporters to go out and vote, and create a sense of urgency that convinces opposition parties to drop unnecessary internal boycotts and act together to ensure positive political change in Israel.”

[_Nimrod Goren_](https://mitvim.org.il/en/team/dr-nimrod-goren/)_, President & Founder, Mitvim Institute; Executive Board Member & Co-Founder, Diplomeds_

## Hamas’ strategic recalculation: from governance of Gaza to the ballot box

“Hamas’ decision to dissolve its governing body and to fully transfer its administrative authority to the NCAG should be read alongside the group’s acceptance, on 30 July, of the Board of Peace’s 15-point roadmap, which ties weapons decommissioning to Israeli withdrawal. Together they mark a strategic recalculation, not a surrender: Hamas is trading the burdens of government and arms for a route back through the ballot box in the supposed November legislative elections. Its electoral alliance with Mohammed Dahlan, the Fatah security chief whose forces it routed in 2007, shows how instrumental its ideology has always been: doctrine bends to survival. The test now is whether Israel allows the NCAG into Gaza to govern, whether decommissioning is verified, and whether the elections produce one Palestinian authority rather than a reshuffled division.”

[_Jaser Abu Mousa_](https://mei.edu/person/jaser-abumousa/)_, Senior Fellow, Middle East Institute_

## Deepening polarisation leaves Israeli society divided ahead of vote

“The Hamas terrorist attack on 7 October 2023 came at an exceptionally delicate moment for Israel. Since January of that year, Israeli society had been deeply divided between those opposing the government’s proposed judicial overhaul – largely secular, centrist and left-leaning segments of the population – and those supporting it. Tensions had escalated to the point of violent incidents, including attacks on protesters, prompting some observers to warn that the country was approaching the brink of civil conflict. 7 October temporarily transformed this picture. In the aftermath of the attack, Israeli society rallied around its flag, displaying a renewed sense of national unity and solidarity. Yet this cohesion proved short-lived, as long-standing divisions gradually resurfaced. From the fate of the hostages held in Gaza, which fuelled mass protests against the government’s handling of the crisis, to the debate over Netanyahu’s responsibility for the failures that enabled 7 October, and the contentious issue of Haredi military conscription, the fractures within Israeli society soon became apparent once more. As elections approach, these divisions remain deeply entrenched. Political and social polarisation continues to shape Israeli public life, and it is difficult to imagine that the electoral outcome alone will be sufficient to overcome them.”

[_Sara Isabella Leykin_](https://www.ispionline.it/it/bio/sara-leykin)_, ISPI MENA Centre_

## Persistent factional divisions threaten to delay Palestinian elections

“One should not overstate the significance of the latest Cairo talks, particularly in relation to the elections announced for the end of November. The main Palestinian factions have yet to demonstrate sufficient openness to addressing the fundamental political differences that have divided them for years. These include the long-standing Fatah-Hamas divide, as well as divisions within Fatah, including with the Fateh Reform current associated with Mohammed Dahlan. Given the depth of these disagreements, it is difficult to see them being resolved within the short timeframe ahead of the proposed elections at the end of November. If anything, the Cairo dialogue could ultimately contribute to postponing the elections, rather than creating the political consensus necessary for them to proceed.”

[_George Zeidan_](https://www.linkedin.com/in/george-zeidan-b2826438)_, Country Director, The Carter Center in Israel and Palestine_

## Settler expansion in the West Bank reaches record levels after 7 October

“The settler movement formally entered the most senior positions of power in the Netanyahu government, accelerating Israel’s control and cantonisation of the West Bank over the last four years at record levels, including through arming settler militias to terrorise Palestinians. Settlements have long become normalised in Israel, but since 7 October there is not a single Jewish political party running for the Knesset that supports the withdrawal from settlements and the establishment of a Palestinian State. With Israelis focused on internal politics and split over whether Netanyahu’s political career will finally be over, the long-standing occupation of the West Bank and settlement enterprise will not play a significant role in voters’ decisions.”

[_Mairav Zonszein_](https://www.crisisgroup.org/who-we-are/people/mairav-zonszein)_, Israel Senior Analyst, International Crisis Group_

## The growing democratic anomaly in EU relations with Israel

“Democratic systems are expected to respond to the issue preferences of citizens. Since October 2023, several opinion polls in European Union member states have consistently shown a significant decline in public support for Israel and a widespread disapproval of its military actions in Gaza, due to the perceived commission of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Public sentiments have significantly shifted even in European countries with historically strong alignment with Israel, including Germany. Surveys show that most European citizens support imposing sanctions or trade restrictions on Israel to change its behaviour. The democratic anomaly manifested in the growing gap between public sentiments and the official policies of several European governments is undermining the EU’s stated values and its capacity to uphold a rules-based international system. Such anomaly ultimately paves the way for the growth of far-right political options, which tend to be aligned with Israel’s policies and practices.”

_[Haizam Amirah Fernandez](https://www.cearc.net/equipo/haizam-amirah-fernandez/), Executive Director, Centro de Estudios Árabes Contemporáneos (CEARC)_

articles.title: Gaza and the choice ahead for Palestinians and Israelis
articles.cleaned_content:
Three years ago, families in southern Israel woke to a nightmare. Parents held safe-room doors shut while their children hid behind them. Young people fleeing a music festival were hunted across open fields. In the Hamas-led attack, about 1,200 people were massacred and 251 taken hostage into Gaza.

October 7 changed Israel profoundly. It shattered assumptions about security and left wounds that remain open to this day. No serious observer should expect Israelis to think about the future as though that day never happened.

The war that followed brought devastation to Gaza on a scale that will shape Palestinian society for years. Tens of thousands of Palestinians lost their lives. Children grew up knowing displacement, and hunger and fear became part of everyday life. Across Gaza, grief settled into homes, schools and neighbourhoods.

Watch Two-state solution 'practically impossible' without Gaza plan, says Mladenov

Having spent much of my professional life working on this conflict, I have become wary of anniversaries. They encourage remembrance but rarely reflection. Every year we repeat familiar arguments, revisit familiar grievances and reaffirm familiar loyalties. Then we move on, leaving unresolved the very questions that produced the tragedy in the first place.

Yet one truth remains difficult to escape: grief has no nationality. A mother in Nir Oz and a mother in Khan Younis may never meet, and they may hold radically different views about this conflict and its causes, but neither needs a lesson in loss.

The question before Israelis, Palestinians and the wider region is not whose suffering matters more. It is whether enough has been learnt to prevent a continuation of the cycle of pain and suffering.

A year ago, the parties accepted a framework intended to move Gaza away from full-scale war. It established a path towards demilitarisation, deradicalistaion, transitional Palestinian governance, Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction. But the hardest part is not agreeing on the destination. It is turning those commitments into realities.

Today there are essentially three possible futures for Gaza.

The first is a return to the familiar and painful cycle. Hamas rebuilds its military capabilities. Israel prepares for the next confrontation. Another ceasefire eventually follows another round of violence, leaving the underlying reality unchanged.

We have seen this many times before. Every round of fighting was meant to restore deterrence. Every truce was presented as a new beginning. Yet the conflict returned because the conditions that produced it never fundamentally changed.

The second future may appear more stable but is ultimately no more promising. Gaza remains suspended in a state of permanent uncertainty. Humanitarian assistance attempts to replace governance. Reconstruction advances slowly, if at all. The world gradually loses interest. There are no dramatic headlines, but there is no meaningful progress either.

History offers little reason to believe that such arrangements endure. Political vacuums rarely remain empty. Despair is a poor foundation for peace and an excellent recruiting tool for extremism.

The third future is more difficult. It is also the only one that offers a genuine path forward .

Its premise offers the best foundation for peace: verified decommissioning of weapons, deradicalisation, accountable Palestinian civilian governance, phased Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction.

The future of Gaza must ultimately be determined by accountable Palestinian civilian institutions, not competing armed factions. Under US President Donald Trump’s Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict , security must be exercised through lawful structures that answer to a civilian transitional authority. Reconstruction must proceed in an environment where weapons have been permanently decommissioned and military infrastructure dismantled, and where investors, donors and ordinary families can have confidence that war is not simply being postponed. That is not simply a technical requirement, it is a political one.

To Israelis, I would offer one observation.

I understand why many hear proposals for withdrawal or transitional administration and think of the failings of the past. The lesson I draw is that withdrawal without durable security and governance arrangement inside Gaza was insufficient. The fundamental question of who legitimately controls force inside Gaza was never properly resolved.

The answer cannot be blind trust. Security arrangements must be verified and enforced. Yet Israelis should also confront an uncomfortable reality. Walls, buffer zones and recurring military operations cannot deliver lasting security if Gaza remains permanently unstable and under the control of armed factions.

A strategy built entirely around managing the next war is not, in the long run, a strategy for peace.

To Palestinians, and to Arabs across the region, I would offer a similarly candid observation.

The destruction of Gaza has generated understandable anger. Many Palestinians also view international initiatives with suspicion. But there is another question that deserves an honest answer.

Has the dominance of armed factions brought Palestinians closer to statehood, prosperity or freedom?

Societies become stronger when institutions function, when schools educate children, when hospitals care for patients and when accountable governance provides services to people. They do not become stronger when decisions about war and peace are concentrated in the hands of armed groups.

Nor can Gaza build a different future without confronting the ideologies and narratives that have normalised violence and extremism. Change cannot be imposed from outside; it must come through education, functioning institutions, economic opportunity and a political horizon that gives young people an alternative to militancy. The Palestinians of Gaza have paid an intolerable price. They deserve a future that demands more from politics than just aid or calls to sacrifice.

The region and the international community also have responsibilities. Gaza cannot make this transition through declarations alone. Security guarantees must be credible, reconstruction must be supported and Palestinian transitional institutions must be given the means to succeed. Commitments made in conference rooms must ultimately translate into change on the ground.

Implementing President Trump’s comprehensive plan, endorsed by UN Security Council resolution 2803, will not be easy. Agreements alone change very little. What matters is implementation, political courage and sustained commitment long after international attention moves elsewhere. The framework exists. Regional partners are engaged. Technical expertise is available. Financial resources can be mobilised.

The question is whether the political will exists.

There will always be those who resist change because new arrangements challenge familiar interests and established sources of influence. Building something new is invariably harder than defending what already exists. Yet leadership is measured precisely by the willingness to choose the harder path.

For generations, this conflict has imposed costs on the entire region. Palestinians and Israelis have borne by far the greatest burden.

While the dead deserve remembrance, the living deserve a future . We can preserve the conditions that repeatedly produce war, or we can begin building the conditions for peace. There is no neutral ground between those alternatives.
